q: Which wars did Sam Kilgore serve in, and what was his role in each?
ans:

In the Confederate Army, Kilgore enlisted at seventeen [2]. His company was moved to Birmingham to build breastworks, and he recalled, "We allus fixes for de battles and builds bridges and doesn't fight much," seeing only occasional skirmishes [2]. 

A year after arriving in Texas, Kilgore joined the "Fed'ral Army for de Indian war" for seven years [4]. He served in the transportation division, where he "drives oxen and mules, haulin' supplies to de forts," traveling to Fort Griffin, Dodge City, and Laramie, Wyoming [4]. 

Later, he served in the Spanish-American War, where he did "com'sary work" [1, 4]. Kilgore reflected that across all these wars, he saw almost no fighting because he "allus works with de supplies" [4].

q: What happened in the fight on Palo Alto Prairie, and what was Ben Kinchlow's role?
ans:

Fifteen of the bandits were killed and one escaped [2]. Kinchlow stated that the captain "put 'em all up together in a pile and sent a message to Brownsville to the authorities" regarding their location [2]. The bandits had roughly two hundred to two hundred and twenty-five stolen cattle with them [2].

Regarding his role, Kinchlow served as a scout who tracked trails; he stated, "by me gettin' out early next mornin' and findin' that trail, I could tell pretty much how old it was" [2]. He tracked their horses toward Santa Lalla, calculating their direction to intercept them [2]. During another encounter on that same pursuit, the captain told him to stay with the horses rather than join the shooting, remarking, "you ain't paid to kill Meskins!" [3].

q: Which radio story about Captain McNelly did Ben Kinchlow confirm?

He explained that the radio's depiction of shipping cattle on steamboats down the Rio Grande was incorrect: "Why, they never was no cattle on the steamboats down the Rio Grande. I just tell you they was no way of shippin' cattle on a steamboat" [1]. He insisted that the boats carried freight, cotton, and passengers, and that any cattle crossed into Mexico were "swum across" instead [1].

q: How did people in these narratives learn they were free, and how quickly?
ans:
Accounts show people learned of their freedom in varied ways and sometimes after considerable delays, as slaveholders often withheld the news. 

Julia Blanks stated her husband’s master delayed telling the slaves until soldiers arrived at the gate; he quickly called them in and claimed he was just "waiting for them all to be there" [1]. 

Tempie Cummins recalled that after freedom was declared, her master refused to tell anyone, intending to "make another crop or two" [5]. Her mother discovered the truth by eavesdropping in the chimney corner, then ran to tell the field hands [5]. 

Sarah Ford remembered Uncle Charley Burns ran into the yard shouting, "'Everybody free, everybody free,'" before soldiers arrived and a captain read a proclamation [2]. 

Molly Harrell remembered an overseer first whispered under their cabin door at night telling her mother she was free "but not to tell nobody" [3, 4]. Right after that, her master read them the paper announcing their freedom [3, 4].

q: What did people drink when real coffee wasn't available?
ans:
Enslaved and formerly enslaved individuals described several different substitutes when real coffee was unavailable. 

Valmar Cormier stated that during the war, when they could not get good French coffee, they made coffee from "coffee weed" by parching it in an iron oven, grinding it, and boiling it in an iron pot [1]. Mary Kindred recalled that during the war people parched "bran and peanuts and okra seed and sich" to make a "right drinkable coffee" [2]. Sarah Ford remembered that during "slave times," they drank "Parched meal" as coffee, noting it was "purty good iffen you know's how" [3]. Ben Kinchlow recounted that because they did not have much coffee, they made "corn-coffee" by taking corn, parching it "right brown," and grinding it up [4, 5].

q: Accounts of confronting or outwitting the Klan or night riders
ans:
Lorenza Ezell recalled hearing Klansmen say they were going to kill "old man Bart." Ezell jumped out a window, took a shortcut through the woods, and warned him, saving his life [1, 5]. Ezell later told a Klansman he played fiddle with, Irving Ramsey, that he recognized him from a tree; after the men saw Ezell would not tell on them, "dey never try whip my daddy or kill Uncle Bart no more" [5].

Sam Kilgore recounted that after night riders burned his mother's house and plundered homes, "Massa Rodgers" and other white men dug a ditch near the road; when the riders approached, "a volley am fired and lots of dem draps off dey hosses," ending the trouble locally [2].

Pierce Harper reported that after Black men complained to the governor about Klan violence, they were issued old muskets to protect themselves [3]. They formed a militia, and when warned the Klan was coming, "They'd hide in the cabins" and killed many Klansmen in the fighting [3, 4].

q: How was illness treated on plantations?
Wedding customs during and after slavery
ans:
Ann Hawthorne reported hearing about "broom-stick marriages," calling them the "law in dem days," though she never saw one herself [1]. Jeff Calhoun described enslaved weddings where a couple received permission from their owners, answered whether they loved each other, and jumped high over a broom held about a foot off the floor so they would not stub a toe, which signified "trouble comin' 'tween you" [2]. Calhoun added that men wore a good pair of pants and shirt for weddings [2]. Conversely, Richard Carruthers stated that an enslaved groom would "slick up his lowers," put on brass-toed shoes, and be married by a preacher "out of the Bible" [3].

After freedom, Harriet Jones married outdoors under an elm tree, wearing a dress from Miss Ellen, red stockings, and new shoes, accompanied by two flower girls [4]. A preacher officiated, asking vows and reciting scripture, after which they signed a book and celebrated with a backyard feast of barbecue pig, sweet potatoes, and pies, where her mother gave her a bridal "luck charm" [4].

Jeptha Choice stated that his mother, Martha, "had been brought here from Serbia," and his father, John, "was from the East Indies" [2]. He explained that both of his parents were brought to the country on a slave boat owned by Captain Adair and sold in New Orleans before being purchased by Master Jezro Choice [2].

q: Folk beliefs, charms, and conjure
ans:
The narratives detail various charms and folk beliefs. William Adams reported that wearing a silver coin, lodestone, or a "salt and pepper mixture in de little sack" around the neck protects against evil power, though it relies on faith [1]. 

Willis Easter wore a dime on his neck and ankle to stop conjuremen from setting tricks, noting the dime turns dark if friends do him wrong [2]. Easter also carried a "jack" charm in red flannel and described finding water or buried money with a V-shaped tree limb [2]. He recalled his mother tying a leather string, dried frog, or nutmeg around teething babies' necks, and noted conjuremen used hair, fingernails, scorpions, and bat wings [4].

Rosanna Frazier described conjurers using graveyard dirt, hair combings, and clay or straw effigies pierced with pins, as well as making "love powder" from boiled love vine leaves [3]. 

Harriet Collins shared remedies like wearing rattlesnake rattles or alligator teeth for teething, putting red pepper in shoes for chills, and wearing a dime around the ankle to prevent leg cramps [5].

q: What happened when patrols caught enslaved people off the plantation without a pass?
ans: Enslaved people caught without a pass faced severe violence and punishment from patrols. Green Cumby stated that if the "patter rolls cotch you without de pass," a person had "some trouble" and "better wish you dead" [1]. Harry Johnson reported that "de paddlerollers would whip you" even for simply crossing the street to see family without a pass [2]. Johnson also recounted an incident where an enslaver deceived a man asking for a pass by writing a note telling the patrol to beat him; as a result, "[d]e paddlerollers beat him nearly to death" [2]. Fred Brown noted that people caught or facing whippings for sneaking off or running away could be "tied down over a barrel and whipped ha'd, till dey draws blood, sometimes" [4]. Brown also recalled another enslaved man who hid under a house from patrols; when they made him come out, he was terrified and had "de quaverment" like a cold dog [4]. In John James's account, when he was caught off the plantation without a pass by horseback riders he called "white caps," he was terrified and questioned [3].

q: What did the patterrollers do when they cotched folks without a pass?
ans: The accounts describe varying punishments by the patterrollers (or paddlerollers). Green Cumby recalled that if they caught someone without a pass, "you better wish you dead, 'cause you would have yourself some trouble" [1]. In another instance, Cumby stated that patterrollers caught a runaway slave who had killed his wife, took him to a man named Henderson, and hanged him [1]. Harry Johnson reported that if you visited your mother across the street without a pass, "De paddlerollers would whip you" [2]. Johnson also recounted a case where an owner wrote a note asking the paddleroller to give the enslaved person "’nough," and the paddlerollers "beat him nearly to death" according to the note's instructions [2]. In contrast, Fred Brown recalled an occasion when an enslaved man ran from the patters and hid under a house; after they found him, "De patters hits him five or six licks and lets him go" [4].

q: Horses frightened and running away with a carriage
ans:
The provided passages do not describe horses becoming frightened and running away with a carriage. 

However, Albert Hill recalled an incident where he was hauling dinner to field workers in a two-wheel cart, and the horse balked [1]. To make it move, he tied a rope with cockleburs to the horse's tail and the cart's shaft and touched the animal with a whip [1]. This provoked the horse to rear back and then bolt to try to get away from its tail, resulting in a runaway cart that rushed straight through a line of workers who were attempting to stop it [1].

q: De hosses skeert and run off with de coach
ans:
Lewis Jones recalled an incident where his enslaver had just changed the gin's power from horses to steam [1]. While Jones was waiting beside the house with the coach team for his mistress to come out, his enslaver was already inside the coach [1, 3].
